Which store gets the last unit?

1 · Problem

Same stock, different outcome: allocation is the decision

  • A warehouse rarely has enough to cover every store. Every unit sent to one store is a unit another store doesn't get.
  • The decision is a whole number of units per store, under warehouse supply, shelf space and per-item caps.
  • In this tiny example, the same 60 units fill 20% more demand just by sending them where they will sell.
This exact example is one of the project's automated tests: the optimiser must find 40 / 20.
Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economics3 / 14
1 · Problem

A better forecast score doesn't guarantee a better decision

  • In this setup, running out costs 6.25 MU per unit; overstocking costs 1.25 MU. Roughly 5 : 1.
  • Accuracy metrics such as MAE treat both errors as equally bad, so a model tuned for accuracy is tuned for the wrong goal.
  • The quantity to measure is the cost of the decision, compared with the best decision possible in hindsight (regret).
Costs are synthetic. In a real deployment they would come from margin, holding and freight data.
Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economics4 / 14
2 · Approach

From history to shipments, with the optimiser in the training loop

Forecast → optimise

Train the forecaster for calibrated probabilities, then optimise. The standard approach and a fair baseline.

Decision-focused learning (DFL)

During training, the optimiser scores each forecast by the cost of the decision it led to (SPO+ loss), and the model learns from that.

Same model, same budget

Both versions share architecture, initial weights, data order and epochs. Only the training signal differs.

Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economics5 / 14
2 · Approach

Risk-aware allocation: plan for the bad weeks, not only the average

  • Simulate many possible next weeks from the forecast, keeping stores' tendency to move together.
  • The robust optimiser gives extra weight to the most expensive scenarios. Mathematically, this equals minimising the average cost of the worst tail of outcomes (CVaR).
  • Two dials: how far into the tail (α) and how much to care about it (risk weight). Both chosen on validation data only: α = 0.75, weight = 0.25.
  • Setting the risk weight to zero gives back the ordinary average-cost plan, a built-in sanity check.
Average-cost plan
every scenario counts equally
Robust plan
expensive scenarios weighted up
Cost: a little more on an average week. Benefit: fewer very bad weeks, if the forecast's uncertainty is right.
This is probability-reweighting robustness. It is not Wasserstein DRO, and I label it that way.
Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economics6 / 14
3 · Analysis

How I made the comparison fair

100 weeks training
8 validation
12 test
Time only moves forward: the model never sees the future it is tested on.

Same conditions

Every policy faces the same weeks, stock, supply, shelf limits and costs.

Two regimes

5 stores × 10 household items each: regular sellers and intermittent sellers.

Strong baselines

Equal split and a proportional rule (last 8 weeks of sales), as a retailer would use.

Checked independently

All 288 policy-week allocations re-verified: feasible, costs recomputed, no negative regret.

Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economics7 / 14
3 · Analysis

Results: big win over equal split; models tie with a simple rule

Read it this way: regular demand, equal split is clearly worst and the rest overlap. Intermittent demand, forecast → optimise is the only policy clearly better than the proportional rule on the primary seed (-7.0 MU, interval [-11.4, -2.5]). Even the best policy is ~279 MU from perfect hindsight, which is the limit of predictability.

Do the rankings survive retraining? Not reliably

5 · Impact

What the evidence supports, and what it doesn't

Supported

  • Demand-aware allocation beats an equal split by about 133 MU/week (9.3%) in this setup, with a clear interval.
  • An open-source integer optimiser handles the constraints in a fraction of a second per week.
  • The evaluation harness catches lucky results: paired intervals, retrained seeds, independent recomputation.

Not supported (yet)

  • That decision-focused learning or robust optimisation beats a simple rule on this data.
  • Any real saving in RM: costs are synthetic and sales stand in for demand.
  • Performance at network scale: this is 5 stores × 10 items per regime.
Recommended next step: run the proportional rule plus optimiser as the baseline, and treat DFL / robust optimisation as challengers that must win a pre-registered shadow test.

5 · Impact

From prototype to pilot: a low-risk path

Phase 1 · Shadow
Weeks 1–8

Connect real stock, sales and cost data. Generate recommendations alongside planners; ship nothing. Measure regret vs current orders.

Go if: clear, significant gain vs current practice
Phase 2 · Pilot
Weeks 9–16

Small store cluster and a focused item set. Planner can override; every override is logged and reviewed.

Go if: fewer stockouts, no rise in overstock
Phase 3 · Scale
After pilot review

Solve items in parallel (each item's warehouse limit is separate), then reconcile shelf space. Monitor drift.

Challenger models promoted only on evidence

B1 · The optimisation model

Cost for one week (per store s, item p)
cost = Σ b · shortagesp + h · leftoversp + t · shippedsp
shortage = max(D − I − x, 0) leftover = max(I + x − D, 0)
Constraints
Σs xsp ≤ Wp (warehouse) Σp (Isp + xsp) ≤ Cs (store space) 0 ≤ xsp ≤ Ksp, integer
Value of the k-th extra unit (exact identity, unit-tested)
c[s,k] = t − b if demand ≥ I + k (it prevents a shortage), else t + h (it is left over)
expected: ĉ[s,k] = t + h − (b + h) · P(D ≥ I + k)

b = 6.0, h = 1.0, t = 0.25 MU per unit (synthetic). Solver: HiGHS (open source). Fulfilment is recomputed after solving as min(demand, stock).

Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economicsBackup

B2 · Decision-focused learning details

SPO+ loss (Elmachtoub & Grigas), used via PyEPO
L(ĉ, c) = maxw∈S (c − 2ĉ)ᵀw + 2ĉᵀw*(c) − c ᵀw*(c)
Training objective
loss = NLL(demand distribution) + λ · SPO+, λ chosen on validation from {0, 0.5, 1, 2}
  • Training uses a fixed set of constraints per item, so SPO+'s assumptions hold. Real weekly limits are applied at decision time.
  • Gradient check: SPO+ gradient is finite and non-zero; λ = 0 vs λ > 0 produce different updates.
  • Validation regret is recomputed after restoring the best checkpoint and calibration.
Interview case study · Walmart M5 sales proxy · synthetic MU economicsBackup

B3 · Why the robust model equals CVaR

Ambiguity set over N scenarios with base probabilities p
Pα = { w : Σ wj = 1, 0 ≤ wj ≤ pj / (1 − α) }
maxw∈Pα Σ wj Lj(x) = CVaRα(L(x))
Objective
min (1 − ρ) · E[L(x)] + ρ · CVaRα(L(x))
  • Solved exactly as one integer program with the standard CVaR linearisation (η, zj).
  • Checked against brute-force enumeration on small cases; α = 0 or ρ = 0 recovers the average-cost plan.
  • Scenarios share random numbers across policies and keep cross-store dependence learned from training weeks only.
